title: Foundations: Honky Tonk - The Complete Guide
summary: What Honky Tonk is, where it came from, and how its songs work.
body:
Honky Tonk songs: Honky-tonk is barroom country: shuffles, Telecaster twang, and songs about cheating, drinking, and dancing. Ernest Tubb and Hank Williams made the honky-tonk the center of country music.

History: Born in Texas dance halls in the 1940s: Ernest Tubb's Walking the Floor Over You (1941), Hank Williams's hits, and Ray Price's shuffle beat. Dwight Yoakam revived it in the 1980s.

How the songs work: Honky Tonk favors the keys of E, A, G, D. Common forms include Shuffle verse-chorus with twin-guitar breaks; Dance-hall two-step tempo. Players should master chicken-pickin' telecaster first, then the ray price shuffle: walking bass under 4/4. Telecaster twang in open positions.

title: Honky Tonk Etude No. 1: Honky-tonk I–V–vi–V
summary: An original Honky Tonk study in A drilling the ray price shuffle: walking bass under 4/4.
body:
This original etude isolates the 'Honky-tonk I–V–vi–V' progression in the key of A — the changes Honky Tonk players must know cold.

CHART:
A | E | F#m | E

FORM: dance-hall two-step tempo.

PRACTICE: loop the chart slowly, adding the ray price shuffle: walking bass under 4/4 once the changes are clean. Then transpose with the included program and drill it in all twelve keys — the Honky Tonk player's rite of passage.

title: Your Cheatin' Heart - Honky Tonk Song Study
summary: Harmonic blueprint and playing guide for Your Cheatin' Heart by Hank Williams (1952).
body:
Your Cheatin' Heart — Hank Williams, 1952. Released after Hank's death; the honky-tonk epitaph.

HARMONIC BLUEPRINT (study chart, key of G):
Gm | Cm | F7 | A#

This study chart uses the 'Cheatin' vi–ii–V–I' progression, the Honky Tonk workhorse, to map how songs like this move. Form: shuffle verse-chorus with twin-guitar breaks. Listen for fiddle breaks between verses — it is the fingerprint of the style.

TO PLAY IT: set your tempo to the Honky Tonk pocket, voice the chords cleanly, and let fiddle breaks between verses. Telecaster twang in open positions. (Song facts: title/artist/year are documented public records; the chart is an original study arrangement.)
